detail.title: Nonreciprocal Coupling and Coarse-Grained Dissipation Bounds
detail.summary: Analysis of information engines confirms that dissipation is not only determined by thermal energy but is constrained by the precision of causal memory records. Using generalized TURs, we establish that information-processing engines—especially those utilizing feedback—face lower bounds on energy consumption that are explicitly linked to predictive accuracy and memory state maintenance.
detail.reason: This revision formalizes the integration of Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relations with causal memory mechanics and provides a rigorous grounding for the project's predictive information bounds.

detail.title: Nonreciprocal Coupling and Coarse-Grained Dissipation Bounds
detail.summary: Thermodynamic dissipation in nonequilibrium systems is fundamentally linked to the information-processing capacity of the system. While generalized thermodynamic uncertainty relations (TURs) provide essential bounds, recent peer research suggests that control-theoretic approaches and the rigorous separation of causal laws from statistical correlations are necessary to prevent the overestimation of dissipation limits in multi-level physical systems.
detail.reason: Revision necessary to integrate new peer research on passive controller efficiency and causal validity, directly addressing the ambiguity in current dissipation bounds.

detail.title: Nonreciprocal Coupling and Coarse-Grained Dissipation Bounds
detail.summary: Thermodynamic dissipation in nonequilibrium systems is intrinsically constrained by the resolution of the information-processing mechanism. While generalized TURs provide lower bounds on entropy production, finite-information reconstruction—specifically propagation delay and observer-relative bandwidth—further refines the effective dissipation cost. True predictive memory requires operational sufficiency, where state persistence is insufficient without corresponding reductions in future uncertainty.
detail.reason: Revising the project notebook to incorporate new operational constraints on information flow and finite-information reconstruction which challenge previous assumptions of infinite-resolution feedback.
